results.title: Nebius Is Raising the Price of Its AI Compute on Oct. 1. Here's What That Says About the Shortage. | The Motley Fool
highlights:
## Key Points

- Nebius' on-demand hourly rates for four Nvidia GPU models climb between 17% and 21% on Oct. 1.
- Management says it could sell all its 2027 capacity today on the terms of its newest contracts.
- The company expects to spend $20 billion to $25 billion on capital expenditures this year.

Nebius Group (NBIS -9.92%) is about to charge more for the computing power it rents out by the hour. On Thursday, Oct. 1, the artificial intelligence (AI) cloud company's on-demand rate for an Nvidia B300 graphics processing unit (GPU) climbs 21%, from $7.85 per hour to $9.50.

Nebius expects to spend $20 billion to $25 billion on capital expenditures this year, versus guided revenue of $3 billion to $3.4 billion. A company building capacity so fast normally needs to work to fill it, not raise prices on it.

...

## Even older chips cost more

The Oct. 1 increase isn't the first this year. In early May, Nebius' pricing page showed the older H100 chip at $2.95 per hour and the B300 at $6.10.

After this round, the same chips will cost $4.50 and $9.50 -- around 53% and 56% more than five months before. This round includes four Nvidia GPUs (the H100, H200, B200, and B300), with hikes of 17% to 21%, plus Nebius' CPU-only servers.

What strikes me is the H100, a generation behind Nvidia's Blackwell chips (the B200 and B300). Rising prices for older hardware arguably say more about a shortage than a premium on the latest chip does. After all, Nebius' second-quarter shareholder letter already reported over 30% higher pricing for older-generation GPUs versus the first quarter.

...

"[W]e sold out of capacity because, as fast as we bring capacity online, we can sell it," CFO Dado Alonso said on the company's second-quarter earnings call in August.

CEO Arkady Volozh went further in the shareholder letter, saying Nebius could sell all its 2027 capacity today on the terms of its newest deals. It's saving some for customers with immediate needs instead. What's more, its first capacity auction cleared at the highest price Nebius has seen for Nvidia's Blackwell chips, 15% over anything it had charged earlier.

results.title: Nebius raises on-demand GPU prices from 1 October | VETTDD
highlights:
Nebius raises on-demand GPU prices from 1 October | VETTDD

# Nebius raises on-demand GPU prices from 1 October

The neocloud’s published price list lifts H100, H200, B200 and B300 hourly rates by 17–21%, and partners reselling AI compute are likely to need to rebase their quotes

Editor Editorial desk, VETTDD · 27 September 2026 · 1 min read

The facts

- Spot prices for preemptible HGX H100 and H200 instances start from $0.79 (£0.60) per GPU-hour, and Nebius says they can change as often as every 15 minutes.
- Nebius’s pricing FAQ gives US dollars as the only currency it accepts.
- Egress and ingress traffic, public IP addresses and Nebius’s managed Kubernetes service are listed as free.

Why it matters

Buyers renting GPU capacity on demand should assume that neocloud prices can rise mid-project and budget with headroom. Where workloads are steady, reserved capacity is now the main way to hold costs, so compare a committed term against the hyperscalers before renewing. UK buyers also carry currency risk on dollar-only billing. Check contracts for how much notice a supplier must give before a rate change and whether in-flight work is protected.

Nebius will charge more for on-demand graphics processing unit (GPU) capacity from 1 October 2026, according to the price list on its website. An Nvidia HGX H100 instance rises from $3.85 (£2.91) to $4.50 (£3.40) per GPU-hour, and an HGX B300 from $7.85 (£5.93) to $9.50 (£7.17).

The rest of the HGX range moves the same way. H200 goes from $4.50 to $5.40 (£4.08) and B200 from $7.15 (£5.40) to $8.50 (£6.42). On the page’s own figures, the four rises run from 17% to 21%. Central processing unit (CPU) instances go up too, with AMD Epyc Genoa starting at $0.13 (£0.10) an hour instead of $0.10. RTX Pro 6000 and L40S prices are unchanged, and the rack-scale GB300 and GB200 NVL72 systems remain price on request.

Silicon UK, which reported the change on 18 September, said it is the company’s second rise in three months, taking B300 pricing up a cumulative 56%, and that memory offerings will rise by 41%. Silicon UK also reported that CoreWeave had said the same day that it was signing new contracts at higher prices. The Nebius page still offers up to 35% off on-demand rates for large clusters reserved for several months.

Sources

1. Nebius, “AI Cloud pricing”, price list, accessed 26 September 2026. https://nebius.com/prices
2. Silicon UK, “AI Cloud Firm Nebius Hikes GPU, CPU Prices”, 18 September 2026. https://www.silicon.co.uk/cloud/ai/nebius-prices-ai-631634

highlights:
Nebius raises Nvidia GPU rental rates up to 21% effective October 1, led by B300 at $9.50/hr · AI Factor News

# Nebius raises Nvidia GPU rental rates up to 21% effective October 1, led by B300 at $9.50/hr

By Neil Rubin, with AI assistance

Published Sep 26, 8:00 PM EDT · Updated Oct 1, 12:08 PM EDT

Why it matters

A supplier raising prices into record capex is the strongest possible signal that AI compute demand still exceeds supply — including for last-gen H100s, up 53% since May. It is bullish for the entire AI infrastructure revenue chain (Nvidia's pricing power, Micron's memory pricing power, datacenter landlords), and it is pure pricing power for neoclouds. The bearish offset is real: it raises the cost floor for AI startups' unit economics, which is exactly why falling inference costs matter to the thesis — someone has to make the math work for the renters. For the overbuild debate, this is bear-case kryptonite in price form: overbuilt markets cut prices; this market raises them.

## Summary Nebius raised on-demand AI compute pricing 17-21% across H100/H200/B200/B300 effective October 1, with the B300 going from $7.85 to $9.50/hour — into a year when it is spending $20-25B in capex on $3-3.4B guided revenue.

results.title: Good news for AI bubble skeptics. The era of being able to short GPU rental prices is finally coming.｜会社員薬剤師の投資判断ノート
highlights:
I saw the news that Nebius is raising its on-demand GPU rental rates again starting October 1st. This applies to select NVIDIA chips, with increases ranging from 17% to 21%. This is the second price hike in three months.

...

How much are H100s, H200s, and B200s being rented for right now, and are prices rising or falling? I thought that if I could check this as easily as checking stock prices, I could directly observe the supply and demand in the AI compute resource market.

...

However, the prices seen here are not "someone's contract unit price." They are figures based on publicly available on-demand rental quotes, standardized by generation. Even for the same H100, there is a large spread depending on the provider. I believe the index is meant to look at the center of the market.

...

I found something interesting while researching further.

CME Group is partnering with Silicon Data to prepare futures linked to H100 and B200 GPU rental prices. The product names are Silicon Data H100 Rental Index Futures and Silicon Data B200 Rental Index Futures. The codes are GPU1 and GPU2. Settlement is in cash, and the contract unit is 730 GPU-hours, which is the computing power of renting one GPU for one month.

The target is not the GPU itself. It is the price of renting the GPU's computing power. Even in the CME's explanation, the content of the index is stated to be the on-demand hourly rate of Neoclouds, not hyperscalers.

The initial plan was for a listing on October 5, 2026. In other words, as of the time of writing this article (end of September 2026), it has not yet been officially listed. It is reported that the CFTC has extended its review and will not make the October 5th deadline. The regulators' reasoning was that the spot market for compute resources is fragmented and opaque.

results.title: Hyperscalers vs Neoclouds for GPUs | Codelace
highlights:
A neocloud is a cloud provider focused on GPU and AI workloads, while a hyperscaler offers GPUs within a broad cloud platform. In a September 2026 neocloud vs AWS GPU comparison, Lambda listed H100 SXM instances at $3.99–$4.29 per GPU-hour by node size, and AWS listed P5 Capacity Blocks at $4.720–$5.191 per H100 accelerator-hour across listed regions. The choice depends on the full machine, available quantity, network, storage, existing cloud services and contract terms, rather than the GPU-hour rate alone.

...

Neocloud is an industry term for an AI-focused cloud provider that offers GPU instances, clusters and related software. CoreWeave, Lambda, Crusoe and Nebius are public examples with published GPU offerings. A hyperscaler such as AWS, Google Cloud or Microsoft Azure provides GPU instances as part of a larger catalog of compute, databases, networking and managed services. Neither label specifies one standard product or service level.

results.title: What it costs to rent an H100, B200 or RTX 4090 in September 2026: live prices from 28 GPU clouds — WPS
highlights:
Live cloud GPU prices from 28 providers, September 2026: cheapest on-demand and spot rates for H100, H200, B200, B300, A100, L40S, L4, RTX 4090 and more, next to hyperscaler prices.

 Dev.to · 2026-09-27 

 

GPU rental prices have not converged. The same card can cost several times more depending on which cloud you rent it from, and the cheapest option changes through the day. We run FastGPU, which pulls prices from 28 GPU clouds (marketplaces, neoclouds, serverless platforms and the hyperscalers) and ranks them cheapest first.

Here is the market as it stood on September 27, 2026 at 04:11 UTC, and the few patterns that decide whether you overpay. Prices move daily, so every figure links to its live page.

## The snapshot 

Cheapest on-demand price per GPU-hour for each card, next to the cheapest on-demand price for the same card at a hyperscaler (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud or Oracle). Every figure in a row comes from that card's live page.

| GPU | VRAM | Cheapest on-demand | Offered by | Cheapest hyperscaler | Gap (hyperscaler / cheapest) | Providers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 SXM | 80 GB | $1.79/hr | Cudo Compute | $5.38/hr (Google Cloud) | 5.38 / 1.79 = 3.0x | 22 |
| H200 | 141 GB | $2.60/hr | GMI Cloud | $7.91/hr (AWS) | 7.91 / 2.60 = 3.0x | 18 |
| B200 | 192 GB | $3.69/hr | DeepInfra | $11.28/hr (Google Cloud) | 11.28 / 3.69 = 3.1x | 16 |
| B300 | 288 GB | $4.89/hr | DeepInfra | $17.80/hr (AWS) | 17.80 / 4.89 = 3.6x | 12 |
| GB200 | 192 GB | $8.00/hr | GMI Cloud | $16.00/hr (Oracle Cloud) | 16.00 / 8.00 = 2.0x | 3 |
| A100 80GB | 80 GB | $0.89/hr | DeepInfra | $3.22/hr (Google Cloud) | 3.22 / 0.89 = 3.6x | 18 |
| L40S | 48 GB | $0.47/hr | Vast.ai | $1.86/hr (AWS) | 1.86 / 0.47 = 4.0x | 13 |
| MI300X | 192 GB | $1.71/hr | TensorWave | none listed | n/a | 4 |
| RTX PRO 6000 | 96 GB | $0.93/hr | Vast.ai | $0.97/hr (Google Cloud) | 0.97 / 0.93 = 1.0x | 11 |
| L4 | 24 GB | $0.11/hr | Vast.ai | $0.71/hr (Google Cloud) | 0.71 / 0.11 = 6.5x | 7 |
| RTX 4090 | 24 GB | $0.14/hr | Vast.ai | none listed | n/a | 4 |
| RTX 5090 | 32 GB | $0.21/hr | Vast.ai | none listed | n/a | 3 |

## 1. Hyperscalers charge 3.0x to 3.6x more for the same flagship silicon 

For the data-center flagships, the cheapest hyperscaler rate is 3.0x the floor on H100 SXM ($5.38/hr vs $1.79/hr), 3.1x on B200 ($11.28/hr vs $3.69/hr) and 3.6x on B300 ($17.80/hr vs $4.89/hr). The widest gap in the table is L4 at 0.71 / 0.11 = 6.5x. You pay the hyperscaler premium for the ecosystem (IAM, networking, managed services, committed-use discounts, startup credits), which can be worth it, but it is a choice rather than a default. The exception is the new workstation-class Blackwell card: an RTX PRO 6000 starts at $0.93/hr (Vast.ai) and costs $0.97/hr on Google Cloud, almost the same.

## 2. Spot capacity is cheaper again, with two catches 

If your job checkpoints, interruptible capacity cuts the price further: H100 SXM from $0.98/hr, H200 from $1.84/hr, B200 from $1.77/hr. The first catch: spot can be reclaimed at any moment, so it suits checkpointed training and offline batch jobs, never a user-facing endpoint. The second: the cheapest listings are often whole nodes. In the open dataset, the H200 spot floor on AWS requires 8 GPUs and the B200 spot floor on Google Cloud requires 8 GPUs, so the real entry ticket is that many times the per-GPU price.

## 3. Blackwell is rentable on demand 

B200 is listed by 16 providers from $3.69/hr (DeepInfra), B300 by 12 from $4.89/hr (DeepInfra), and GB200 by 3 from $8.00/hr (GMI Cloud). If you assumed the newest silicon was contact-sales only, much of it now has a public hourly price.

...

## 5. The floor moves, so check it when you rent 

Marketplace prices change as hosts come and go, and a cheap listing can be rented out within the hour. Each GPU page carries a 30-day price strip showing the low, the typical price and whether now is a good moment to rent (for example H200 or L40S).

## How to choose, in four steps 

1. Size the VRAM your model needs first. Everything else follows from it.
2. Decide whether the job tolerates interruption. Checkpointed training can use spot; an endpoint cannot.
3. Compare the landed cost, not the headline rate. Minimum GPU counts, egress, storage and cold-start billing can erase a cheap rate.
4. Check availability. A price with no stock behind it is not a price.

...

## Method and disclosure 

Prices are USD per GPU-hour, read from each provider's public API or pricing page and refreshed continuously. "Cheapest on-demand" counts on-demand and community listings, preferring ones that are not sold out; spot, reserved and serverless are shown separately. The hyperscaler reference is the cheapest on-demand offer for that card at AWS, Azure, Google Cloud or Oracle. Snapshot taken September 27, 2026 at 04:11 UTC; the linked pages show the current numbers. Some provider links on FastGPU are affiliate links; price tables and every "cheapest" figure here are ordered strictly by price.
